findings.claim: The city's December 2025 committee deck states the program's scale: 100 AI-enabled cameras on sanitation brush trucks.
findings.quote: Implement 100 AI-enabled cameras on Sanitation brush trucks
findings.source_type: primary_official (city deck, slide 3, read from rendered pages)
findings.why_it_matters: The first city-stated number in the chain and the baseline for any 'first citations' comparison. Slide 4 gives two cameras per vehicle, so 100 cameras implies 50 vehicles; that is arithmetic from the slides, labelled as derived, and it matches press reports of 50 trucks.

findings.claim: The camera takes photos while the truck drives at street speed. This matters because the catalog's street-capture action is stationary.
findings.quote: Take photos as it drives (25-35 MPH)
findings.source_type: primary_official (slide 4)
findings.why_it_matters: Sets the true physical action for the opening: a moving vehicle at 25 to 35 miles per hour, two cameras on one city vehicle. A stationary illustration would misstate the mechanism.

findings.claim: The side-facing cameras capture from the public right-of-way and blur faces and plates.
findings.quote: Captures images from the public right-of-way; Automated blurring of personal information (license plate numbers and faces)
findings.source_type: primary_official (slide 5). Note: the two quoted phrases are separate bullets on slide 5 and are joined here for brevity.
findings.why_it_matters: Privacy is the city's first answer to the surveillance objection. A film that shows faces must follow this, and a film that shows a readable plate can't claim this.

findings.claim: The detection list runs well beyond trash and includes housing condition.
findings.quote: Bulk trash participation; Collapsing structures; Trash; Tires; Illegal dumping; Graffiti; Boarded windows/doors; High Grass; Housing Condition
findings.source_type: primary_official (slide 6). Items joined with semicolons here for brevity; the slide lists them as bullets.
findings.why_it_matters: The camera is described as detecting property condition, not only curb trash. That is the source of the sharpest human stake, and it explains why one of the film's images should be a house, not only a pile.

findings.claim: The city says the system is not automated ticketing and that a human is in the loop for all actions.
findings.quote: NOT automated ticketing; There is a human in the loop for all actions
findings.source_type: primary_official (slide 12)
findings.why_it_matters: This is the city's own test. The film has to show the chain from flag to notice to inspection to citation and let the viewer judge the claim. The viewer is not told the answer in advance.

findings.claim: The city's own framing of the capture is 'just like Google Street View'.
findings.quote: Public right-of-way image capture; Just like Google Street View
findings.source_type: primary_official (slide 12)
findings.why_it_matters: The counter-image. The city's comparison is a useful and checkable frame: street-level imagery of a whole neighborhood, which a homeowner did not ask for and a notice then uses. Use the city's words only as the city's claim.

findings.claim: The contract cost is $852,000 per year, which includes 100 cameras and all associated technology, installation, data services, maintenance, warranty, and replacement support.
findings.quote: The contract cost is $852,000 per year, which includes 100 cameras and all associated technology, installation, data services, maintenance, warranty, and replacement support.
findings.source_type: primary_official (city memo of November 21st, 2025, page 2; also on the December deck slide 8)
findings.why_it_matters: The primary source for the $852,000 per year figure the press repeats. Press also says $2.5 million or $2.56 million, which is the three-year estimate, so the film should say a three-year estimate of $2,556,000 and an annual cost of $852,000.

findings.claim: The contract is a three-year service contract with a one, one-year renewal option. Press accounts left the renewal out.
findings.quote: It authorizes a three-year service contract with a one, one-year renewal option with City Detect for the purchase, installation, training and support of AI-powered camera technology for the Department of Sanitation and Code Compliance Services for an estimated amount of $2,556,000.
findings.source_type: primary_official (city memo, Nov 21st, 2025, page 1)
findings.why_it_matters: The program is designed to continue. Its exit is a ten day notice, so the October 19th briefing can change the contract without a new vote only if the city chooses to. The renewal line belongs in the film's who-can-act frame.

findings.claim: Data retention is set by the contract, which conflicts with the one-year figure in the press.
findings.quote: City Detect maintains the data for the duration of the contract. The City of Dallas may download and retain the data during the term of the agreement and for 90 days following its termination.
findings.source_type: primary_official (city memo, Nov 21st, 2025, page 1; the first sentence is read from the page text and the second sentence is from the same answer)
findings.confidence: high for the city's Nov 2025 position; unresolved against the press's one-year figure
findings.why_it_matters: Storage length is a privacy fact a viewer will ask about. The press says images are retained for one year (NBC and Dallas Express). The city's November memo says the contract retention runs for the term plus 90 days. Both can't be true of the same data unless the policy changed, so the film must not state a retention period.

findings.claim: The Dallas Police Department has no direct access, and the contract is solely between Sanitation and Code Compliance.
findings.quote: No. The Dallas Police Department will not have direct access. The contract is solely between Sanitation Services and Code Compliance.
findings.source_type: primary_official (city memo, Nov 21st, 2025, page 2)
findings.why_it_matters: Defines the enforcement chain: Code Compliance owns the notices. A film that shows a police car or a dispatcher would be a false implication.

findings.claim: The city's December 10th release reports council approval and states the curb-line capture.
findings.quote: The Dallas City Council has approved the deployment of artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled cameras. side-mounted cameras will periodically take still photos of the curb line visible from the public right-of-way.
findings.source_type: primary_official (City of Dallas news release, COM/311, December 10th, 2025). Read through a tool summary of the page, so the exact punctuation of the dash in AI-enabled should be checked against the bytes before any on-screen use.
findings.why_it_matters: The strongest primary text for the mechanism the opening needs: side-mounted stills of the curb line, not a moving video. It is the city's own description of what is captured.

findings.claim: The city's December 10th release calls Dallas the largest city in the nation to use the technology. This is a city claim, not verified.
findings.quote: Dallas is the largest city in the nation to employ this technology.
findings.source_type: primary_official (city claim)
findings.confidence: high that the city said it; not verified
findings.why_it_matters: A scale claim that a film should attribute, not repeat. The Docket and the press do not test it.

findings.claim: City records show the cameras scored more than 21,000 properties in four months, and the city told NBC it had sent 1,800 courtesy notices.
findings.quote: An NBC 5 investigation uncovered city records showing the cameras scored more than 21,000 properties in four months. ... it has already sent 1,800 notices, which it calls "courtesy notices,"
findings.source_type: journalism (NBC 5 Investigates, Sept 2nd, 2026; fetched through the tool, and the Docket marks NBC's site as barring automated readers, see defect D12)
findings.confidence: medium (press; body text returned to my fetch; Docket access flag applies)
findings.why_it_matters: Gives a second unit of measure (properties scored) that is not the 10,000 scanned figure from the memo. The film must not merge these. The 1,800 notice count is the city's own early figure and conflicts with the later 3,700.

findings.claim: The city's stated goal for notices is about 5,200 per year.
findings.quote: its goal was to issue about 5,200 notices per year.
findings.source_type: journalism (NBC, quoting a city statement)
findings.why_it_matters: The stated target is a notice volume, not an enforcement outcome. A film can say the city's goal was a notice volume without calling the program a success or failure.

findings.claim: The notices ask residents to make repairs voluntarily, and the press reports they can lead to enforcement and fines if unresolved.
findings.quote: The notices ask residents to make repairs voluntarily. ... If the problems are not addressed, the warning can eventually lead to additional enforcement and fines.
findings.source_type: journalism (NBC, reporter's own description; it calls the notice a warning)
findings.why_it_matters: The reporter calls the notice a warning, the city says it is not a warning, and the code official says you could call it one. The film must show the disagreement rather than take a side.

findings.claim: The City Detect CEO says faces and plates are blurred and the cameras are not tied to a database. NBC reports the vendor has no say in the city's enforcement use.
findings.quote: We blur faces. We blur license plates. We're not tied in to any database.
findings.source_type: journalism (NBC, quoting the vendor CEO Gavin Baum-Blake)

findings.quote: My primary concern is that this could end up being inadvertently a tax on the poor,
findings.source_type: journalism (NBC, quoting Councilmember Chad West)

findings.quote: In a memo written last week addressing questions about the cameras, City Manager Kimberly Bizor Tolbert wrote that "57 citations have been issued at 34 properties for non-compliance," so far.
findings.source_type: journalism quoting a primary memo that was NOT retrieved. NBC's body was returned by my fetch, but the Docket marks NBC as access-restricted (see D12).

findings.quote: A September 8 memo from the City of Dallas detailed the findings and costs (Fox 4, partial). A September 8 city memo says ... 57 citations have been issued at 34 properties after camera detections were reviewed and confirmed by code officers. (Dallas Express)
findings.source_type: journalism (Fox 4, Sept 18th, 2026, Lori Brown; Dallas Express, Sept 21st, 2026, guest author). The memo date comes from these two outlets only, and NBC says only 'last week' relative to September 17th.

findings.source_type: journalism reporting the memo

findings.quote: 39 citations, or 68%, were issued in City Council Districts 4, 8 and 7 in Southern Dallas. (Dallas Express, attributed to the memo). The NBC version: "The city manager's memo said 39 of those citations, or 68%, were issued to people in City Council Districts 4, 8 and 7 in Southern Dallas." (per docket transcript; the fetch confirmed the phrase '39 of those citations, or 68%')
findings.source_type: journalism reporting the memo (Dallas Express, Sept 21st, 2026)

Dallas Express: The city also sent approximately 3,700 property owners what it calls "courtesy notices" after potential violations were detected.
findings.source_type: journalism reporting the memo (Fox 4); the Dallas Express wording is a separate outlet's reading of the same figure

filmability.viewer_question: When a camera on a city truck flags a yard, who decides it's a violation?
filmability.opening_action: A sanitation truck passes a curb pile at 25 to 35 miles per hour, labelled as an illustration of the city's stated speed. A side-mounted camera takes one still of the curb line, and that still becomes the first step in the chain.
filmability.mechanism: Mechanism-led chain, in the city's and the press's own order: (1) a side-mounted still of the curb line from the public right-of-way (city, Dec 9th deck and Dec 10th release); (2) software flags of property conditions from the city's list, including bulk trash participation, tires, illegal dumping and boarded windows (city deck, slide 6); (3) a code compliance analyst reviews the observation (DMN); (4) a courtesy notice goes to the owner, which the city says is not a warning and which asks the owner to correct the violations to avoid further enforcement action (NBC, unconfirmed); (5) a code officer inspects the property in person before any citation (memo as reported by Fox 4 and Dallas Express); (6) the memo's count: 57 citations at 34 properties, 39 of them in Districts 4, 8 and 7 (as reported).
filmability.human_consequence: A homeowner in southern Dallas who receives a notice headed 'violations identified' is asked to correct it to avoid further enforcement action. The city and its code official disagree about whether that letter is a warning. The press reports that councilmembers worry the cost could fall on lower-income owners, which is a stake and not an outcome. No sourced account of a specific owner's outcome was found, and no named resident is used here.
filmability.source_limit: The strongest limit is that the September 8th memo, which carries every outcome figure, was not retrieved and exists in the record only through press. The press counts disagree by unit (10,000 scanned, 21,000 scored, 20,000 code concerns, and 21,000 addresses) and by notice total (520, 1,800, about 3,700 and almost 4,000 headline). The notice wording rests on one outlet that the Docket marks unconfirmed. Data retention conflicts: the city says term plus 90 days, the press says one year. The October 19th committee materials were not found and the outcome of the briefing is not known at the research date.
three_key_images: 1. A side-mounted camera on a sanitation truck photographs a curb line from the public street at 25 to 35 miles per hour. Original illustration, disclosed; the speed and curb-line capture are the city's own words.

2. A notice sheet with 'violations identified' in bold near the top and 'Please correct the violations promptly to avoid further enforcement action' below. Original layout of quoted wording; disclosed as a reconstruction of the press's quoted text, since no primary copy was retrieved.

3. Text-only card with two city sentences side by side: 'NOT automated ticketing' from the city's own deck (slide 12) against 'A courtesy notice is not a warning or a violation' from the city manager's memo as quoted by NBC, then the code official's 'you could call that a warning' as an on-screen quote. Source-excerpt rendering, words preserved.

asset_leads.asset: City deck slide 5: side-facing camera on a sanitation truck, plus an inset labelled 'Mounted City Detect Camera'
asset_leads.relevant_image: truck photograph with a roof box, labelled SA101 on the door; inset product image of the camera
asset_leads.what_it_proves: The camera's form factor and mounting on a city-type vehicle, as the city presents it. It does not prove which truck is shown, the truck's operator, or that it is a Dallas capture.
asset_leads.rights_or_attribution_evidence: City of Dallas council material; no licence statement seen on the page. The inset product image has no credit. Rights not established. Retrieved only as a rendered page, no image file or hash was extracted.
asset_leads.native_illustration_more_honest: Yes for the capture and mount. Use an original illustration, labelled as illustration, unless a licence for the city's photo is confirmed.

asset_leads.asset: City deck slide 7: software portal map and a 'What City Detect will see' still of a side-view house with an on-image timestamp and coordinate text

asset_leads.what_it_proves: The still format carries a date and a location overlay. It does not identify the location of the building. The portal map's colours are not labelled, so they must not be read as severity.
asset_leads.rights_or_attribution_evidence: City deck. Image credit and licence not shown. The slide does not say where or when the still was taken. Vendor involvement is implied by the slide title.

visual_stakes.affected_group: Southern Dallas owners whose houses or yards are photographed from the street, and the owners in Council Districts 4, 8 and 7 who the memo reportedly says received 39 of 57 citations. No individual is named or used.
visual_stakes.physical_subject: a side-mounted camera on a sanitation brush truck, the curb line it photographs, and the notice sheet that comes back
visual_stakes.visible_change: the truck passes at 25 to 35 miles per hour and one still is taken; the still is flagged for a person to review; a notice sheet reading 'violations identified' comes out
visual_stakes.consequence: the owner is asked to correct the violation to avoid further enforcement action; per the memo as reported, a code officer must inspect the property in person before a citation
visual_stakes.question: When a camera on a city truck flags a yard, who decides it's a violation?
visual_stakes.answer: A person reviews the flag and an officer inspects in person before a citation, according to the city and the memo as reported. The first letter still asks the owner to fix the violation to avoid enforcement, and the Code Compliance assistant director said you could call that a warning. The October 19th briefing outcome is not reported.
visual_stakes.asset_fit: weak for real pictures: no authenticated Dallas capture, parcel, notice or inspection image was retrieved with a licence. The city's deck images are unlicensed and mostly vendor-made. Original illustration is the honest route for the capture, the notice and the flow.

viewer_plan.medium_choice: News report with an explanatory animation as the primary approach (original illustration of the sequence) and source-excerpt text for the quotes. Evidence-led imagery is limited to the quoted words. Observed documentary was rejected because no authenticated Dallas footage was retrieved. A cinematic scene was rejected because the only human steps (review, inspection) would need invented people.
viewer_plan.structure: mechanism-led, with a human-led close only if a sourced person is available; none is used here
viewer_plan.plausible_alternative_rejected: a cinematic scene of an inspector at a door, rejected: no source shows the inspection, and a synthetic officer would imply an observed event
viewer_plan.likely_false_inference: that the truck writes the citations, or that AI found 57 code violations. The memo, as reported, says citations come after a camera flag is reviewed and confirmed by code officers, and only after an in-person inspection
viewer_plan.limit_on_screen: every outcome count is labelled as reported from a city memo dated September 8th, which was not retrieved
viewer_plan.spoken_concept_without_truthful_picture: 'a code compliance analyst reviews the observation' and 'a code officer inspects the property in person'. No authenticated picture of either exists in the record, so the film may show them only as labelled steps, with no people drawn.
viewer_plan.information_sequence: 1 the truck and the still (illustration); 2 the flag categories (city list, text); 3 the review step (labelled step); 4 the notice (quoted words, illustration); 5 the city's 'not a warning' against the official's 'you could call that a warning' (quotes); 6 the inspection step (labelled step); 7 the memo's count with its source and districts (text); 8 the close: the October 19th briefing and the two things the city says it can't yet show, namely savings and enforcement improvement (DMN).

rejected_alternatives.story: FMCSA exemption letting Level 4 driverless trucks, including Aurora, use cab-mounted beacons instead of warning triangles (effective October 7th, 2026)
rejected_alternatives.why_it_is_the_strongest_alternative: If the Dallas pictures can't carry the mechanism, this one has a visible physical contrast: a beacon on the cab in place of triangles on the pavement. It can be drawn as an illustrated truck without a human.
rejected_alternatives.concrete_reason_weaker: The Texas tie is indirect. The notice names no Texas route, and the Texas link is the Texas Trucking Association's support and the fact that driverless trucks run on Texas interstates. The safety finding is a federal judgment on 'likely as safe', so the picture would show a light, not an observed result. The OOIDA objection concerns study design, which can't be pictured.

defects.severity: blocking for any outcome figure on screen
defects.defect: The September 8th memo, which carries every outcome figure (57 citations, 34 properties, 39 in Districts 4, 8 and 7, 10,000 scanned, 3,700 violations), was not retrieved. Every such figure is press-reported (NBC, Fox 4, Dallas Express), and the Docket record says the memo is not published at an address a reader can open. Required: label each figure as reported from the memo by a named outlet, and hold the memo's wording out of any quotation.

The scale figures use different units and don't reconcile: 10,000 properties scanned (Fox 4, citing the memo); more than 21,000 properties scored in four months (NBC, citing city records, Sept 2); roughly 21,000 addresses with potential violations (NBC, Sept 17); more than 20,000 code concerns photographed (DMN); about 13,800 of the 20,000 images in southern Dallas (DMN analysis). Required: name one unit per figure with its source, or drop the figure.

Notice totals conflict: 1,800 notices sent (city to NBC, Sept 2); about 520 courtesy notices June to August (city to DMN); approximately 3,700 property owners sent courtesy notices (Dallas Express, city); 3,700 violations that led to notices (Fox 4, memo); almost 4,000 notices (Fox 4 headline); a 5,200 per year goal (city to NBC). The film must not show a notice total.

Data retention conflicts. The city's November 21st, 2025 memo says City Detect maintains the data for the contract's duration, and the city may download and retain it for 90 days after termination. NBC and Dallas Express say images are expected to be retained for one year. No storage period may be stated until the city resolves it.

The notice wording ('violations identified' in bold, and 'Please correct the violations promptly to avoid further enforcement action') rests only on NBC, which the Docket marks as unconfirmed. Fox 4 and Dallas Express do not repeat it. No primary copy of the notice was retrieved. The notice graphic is blocked until a second source or the city's own form confirms the words.

defects.severity: should be fixed in the Docket record
defects.defect: Docket claim tx-2026-0179-c10 gives the Fox 4 sentence as a verbatim quote ending 'resulting in notices from the city.' My fetch confirmed the start of the sentence, and Fox 4's summary says the sentence continues that the violations led to notices. The tail was not confirmed word for word.

The October 19th committee agenda and briefing materials were not found on any city page retrieved. The outcome of today's briefing is not reported in any source. The film must say the briefing is scheduled or held and must not describe what was said.

The catalog's street-capture-v1 action is stationary (a side camera capturing a residential facade). Dallas captures while driving at 25 to 35 miles per hour. Using street-capture-v1 would misstate the mechanism. The opening must use curb-selection-v1, which is a partial fit, or a new source-backed proposal for a moving capture.

Camera and truck counts. The deck says 100 AI-enabled cameras and two cameras per vehicle, so 50 vehicles, and the press says 50 trucks. The 50 is arithmetic from the deck, not a city-stated figure. Also the press says the contract is $2.5 million, $2.56 million or $2,556,000 over three years, and $852,000 per year. The film should use the city memo's wording.

A search summary (not a fetched page) described NBC coverage with a blight score running from 1 (least severe) to 4 (most severe). It was not confirmed in any fetched body, and NBC's September 2nd body states no blight score scale. Do not use the 1 to 4 scale.

The hearing date moved. NBC's September 2nd report says the city manager agreed to a hearing in December, and NBC's September 17th report says the matter is now scheduled for October. The film can say this, but it must cite the two dates.
